title: Keeping Pace with Ever-Increasing Data: Towards Continual Learning of Code Intelligence Models
core_idea: Representative exemplar replay plus adaptive parameter regularization whose strength scales with old-new dataset similarity
metrics: BLEU-4; ROUGE-L; METEOR; Precision; Recall; F1; Omega; Training time
metrics_display: BLEU / ROUGE-L / METEOR; F1; Average incremental performance; Training time
q1_assessment: The update requirement is motivated by growing code repositories and operationalized mainly as constructed streams of existing projects or algorithm groups. A separate Big-Vul experiment uses dated periods, while the main project partitions do not establish chronological software evolution.
q1_evidence: Sec. IV-A, Fig. 4 and Table I (PDF pp. 5-6) randomly partition CodeSearchNet and Big-Vul projects into five groups and partition POJ functionalities into five groups. Sec. VI-A and Table VII (PDF pp. 9-10) additionally evaluate a programming-language sequence and five Big-Vul periods spanning before 2012 to 2019; Sec. VI-D (PDF p. 11) acknowledges missing chronology in the main partitions.
q2_assessment: Sequential fine-tuning baselines establish a concrete forgetting problem for the evaluated CodeBERT and CodeT5 settings. They do not establish that each incoming project's or algorithm group's knowledge was absent from the backbone before adaptation.
q2_evidence: Fig. 1 (PDF p. 1) shows CodeBERT's first-dataset performance degrading after later updates. Sec. V-A, Tables II-IV and Fig. 5 (PDF p. 7) compare fine-tuning, REPEAT and cumulative retraining for summarization, vulnerability detection and clone detection; the first-dataset curves directly expose lost performance. Secs. IV-A and IV-C (PDF pp. 5-6) specify constructed partitions and pre-trained backbones without a per-stage initial-competence screen.
q3_assessment: REPEAT improves incremental task performance and reduces earlier-task degradation in the tested streams. Summary-agreement and classification metrics support those tasks; no executable program-generation claim is evaluated. A held-out fifth group supplies separate within-task generalization evidence for CodeBERT, while preservation outside the evaluated tasks is not tested.
q3_evidence: Secs. IV-B and V-A, Tables II-IV and Fig. 5 (PDF pp. 5-7) report BLEU/ROUGE, classification F1 and earlier-task trajectories; Eq. 9 aggregates seen-task performance across stages rather than isolating forgetting. Sec. V-B and Table V (PDF p. 8) train on the first four groups and test the fifth using CodeBERT, with Java summarization, vulnerability detection and clone detection. Sec. VI-D (PDF p. 11) limits conclusions to the tested models, tasks and partitions.

title: On the Usage of Continual Learning for Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Pre-trained Language Models of Code
core_idea: Systematic study of Replay EWC SI and RWalk under a stream of API domains
base_models: Code-pretrained GPT-2-like decoder; Code-pretrained RoBERTa-like encoder
metrics: Exact Match@1/5/10; Exact Match; BLEU; CodeBLEU; Average incremental performance; Forgetting
edited_models: Code-pretrained GPT-2-like decoder; Code-pretrained RoBERTa-like encoder
metrics_display: Exact Match@1/5/10; Exact Match; BLEU; CodeBLEU; Average incremental performance; Forgetting
q1_assessment: The requirement is experimentally constructed to simulate incoming unfamiliar API domains using real Java code. Five selected domains are excluded from controlled pre-training and introduced sequentially; the stream is not a trace of actual API releases or deprecations.
q1_evidence: Secs. 3.1-3.2, Fig. 2 and Table 1 (PDF pp. 3-4) construct General, Security, Android, Web and Guava datasets from GitHub methods, select domain-specific interfaces, exclude cross-domain samples and separate OOD data from pre-training data. The GPT-2-like decoder and RoBERTa-like encoder are pre-trained from scratch to control API exposure.
q2_assessment: Controlled exposure and the decoder's zero-shot ID/OOD comparison directly establish an adaptation gap on the selected API tasks. Sequential fine-tuning also demonstrates forgetting in both architectures; the encoder has no comparable zero-shot generation test because its generation head is newly initialized.
q2_evidence: Sec. 4.1 and Tables 2-3 (PDF pp. 5-6) report lower decoder API-call and API-usage scores on every OOD domain than on ID data. Sec. 3.2 (PDF p. 4) and Sec. 4.1 (PDF p. 5) explain the encoder's newly initialized head and exclusion from zero-shot evaluation. Sec. 4.2, Table 4 and Fig. 4 (PDF pp. 6-7) show earlier-domain degradation under naive fine-tuning for both models.
q3_assessment: The experiments support adaptation to the five introduced domains and reduced forgetting with several replay or regularization strategies, with method-dependent trade-offs. Held-out API predictions assess within-domain generalization and earlier-domain retention, using reference agreement rather than execution. Broader code capability preservation and generalization to additional domains are not established.
q3_evidence: Sec. 3.2 (PDF p. 5) defines EM@k for API calls and EM/BLEU/CodeBLEU for API usage. Sec. 4.3, Figs. 5-6 and Tables 5-6 (PDF pp. 7-9) compare adaptation scores and forgetting, finding benefits for replay, SI and RWalk while EWC is weaker and cumulative replay can impair the final domain. Sec. 5.1 (PDF pp. 8-9) limits the study to Java, selected domains, two downstream tasks, five stages and small models.

title: CIRCLE : Continual Repair across Programming Languages
core_idea: Prompt-based data representation with difficulty-based example replay sampled EWC and cross-language re-repairing
metrics: Correct patches; Plausible patches; Validation loss; Unique bugs fixed
metrics_display: Correct patches; Plausible patches; Validation loss; Unique bugs fixed
q1_assessment: The update requirement is a constructed expansion of repair service coverage across programming languages, motivated by incoming service needs. Existing bug-fix corpora are presented in a popularity-based language curriculum, with established repair benchmarks used for evaluation.
q1_evidence: Sec. 1 (PDF p. 2) motivates adding languages as repair-service requirements grow. Sec. 4.2 (PDF p. 6) uses CoCoNut bug-fix data, removes Java commits after 2006 and defines a sequential four-language curriculum covering C, Java, JavaScript and Python. Sec. 4.4 (PDF p. 7) identifies BugAID, QuixBugs, Defects4J and ManyBugs as the evaluation resources.
q2_assessment: The sequential Finetuned-APR baseline demonstrates loss of previously learned repair ability, and generated mismatch examples establish a concrete cross-language output problem. The curriculum itself does not establish that each language was unknown to the starting T5 model before its training stage.
q2_evidence: Secs. 4.4 and 5.1 (PDF p. 7) define the same-backbone baseline and compare current- and earlier-language repairs after each stage; Fig. 4 (PDF p. 9) shows deterioration in earlier-language results. Sec. 3.6 (PDF p. 6), Figs. 7-10 (PDF p. 10) document keyword, formatting and rare-symbol errors before re-repairing. Sec. 3.3 (PDF p. 5) starts from pre-trained t5-base without a language-by-language initial-competence test.
q3_assessment: CIRCLE supports improved repair and partial retention across the four-language curriculum, with residual forgetting visible. Defects4J combines test-passing patches with manual semantic checking; the other benchmark counts use exact agreement with developer patches. A Python-only comparison gives limited cross-language transfer evidence, while broader unaffected-task preservation and unseen-language generalization are not tested.
q3_evidence: Sec. 4.3 (PDF p. 7) defines plausible patches by test passing and correct patches by unanimous semantic review by three authors. Sec. 5.2 and Table 2 (PDF pp. 7-8) report 64 correct/182 plausible Defects4J patches and mark the remaining benchmark counts as exact-match lower bounds. Sec. 5.1 and Fig. 4 (PDF pp. 7, 9) track repair counts on earlier languages and the residual gap to the observed-best upper bound; the Python-only model fixes 21 bugs versus 23 for sequential fine-tuning and 28 for CIRCLE after Python training.

title: Exploring Continual Learning for Code Generation Models
core_idea: Prompt pooling with teacher forcing stabilizes prompt selection over a frozen CodeT5 backbone
baselines: Sequential FT; Individual Models; Multitask; Shared Prompt Tuning; Task-Specific Prompt Tuning; Experience Replay
q1_assessment: The requirement is an experimentally constructed sequence of existing generation, translation, summarization and refinement tasks with sharply different input/output domains. Software evolution motivates the study, but the benchmark does not encode particular library updates or a chronological deployment stream.
q1_evidence: Secs. 3.1-3.2 (PDF pp. 2-3) assemble CONCODE, CodeTrans, CodeSearchNet and bug-fix pairs into CODETASK-CL. Table 1 (PDF p. 4) gives the generation-to-translation-to-summarization-to-refinement sequence; Appendix A.1 (PDF p. 8) describes this as a selected random task order, and Table 2 (PDF p. 9) specifies the language pairs and splits.
q2_assessment: The evaluated CodeT5-small baselines establish severe interference and forgetting under this task sequence, including unstable prompt selection. These measurements diagnose the continual-training problem; they do not establish that every incoming task capability was absent before adaptation.
q2_evidence: Table 1 and Sec. 5.2.1 (PDF p. 4) show low retained performance and high validation-set forgetting for sequential fine-tuning and prompt pooling compared with individual-task and multitask baselines. Sec. 5.2.2 and Fig. 2 (PDF p. 5) trace prompt keys moving toward successive tasks. Appendix A.1 (PDF p. 8) identifies the pre-trained CodeT5-small backbone and frozen-backbone prompt experiments; no per-task pre-adaptation capability screen is reported.
q3_assessment: PP-TF improves BLEU and reduces forgetting relative to unconstrained prompt pooling, while full-model experience replay is stronger in the tested setting. Earlier-task BLEU provides retention evidence, but BLEU does not verify functional correctness of generated, translated or refined programs. Generalization is limited to held-out examples of the four trained tasks in one reported run and order.
q3_evidence: Sec. 3.2 (PDF p. 3) defines all task scores using BLEU and forgetting using historical-best versus final performance. Table 1 (PDF p. 4) reports test-task BLEU and validation forgetting, including 1.68 for PP-TF versus 27.43 for prompt pooling. Appendix A.1 (PDF p. 8) specifies a single run and the evaluation splits; Table 3 (PDF p. 9) examines replay-buffer size without adding execution-based or unseen-task evaluations.

title: SkillLearnBench : Benchmarking Continual Learning Methods for Agent Skill Generation on Real-World Tasks
setting: Task-specific skill refinement and instance reuse
core_idea: Evaluates task-specific skill generation and feedback-based refinement on 20 mixed-domain tasks, with reuse on held-out instances through a fixed solver
base_models: Fixed solver: Claude-Sonnet-4.6; skill generators: Claude-Haiku-4.5, Claude-Sonnet-4.6, Claude-Opus-4.6, Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite, Gemini-3-Flash, Gemini-3.1-Pro; judge: GPT-5-mini
baselines: One-Shot; Self Feedback; Teacher Feedback; Skill Creator; No Skill; Human-authored
metrics: Skill coverage; Executability; Safety; Trajectory alignment; Skill usage rate; Task accuracy; Solving token cost
metrics_display: Skill coverage; Executability; Safety; Skill usage; Task accuracy; Token cost
q1_assessment: The benchmark constructs skill-dependent tasks from community usage categories, adapting existing tasks and adding new ones. The update target is an external task-specific skill document refined from a seed instance and reused on variants, rather than a model-weight update or a demonstrated sequence of transfers between task types.
q1_evidence: Sec. 3.1 and Table 1 (PDF pp. 3-4) define 20 tasks across 15 sub-domains, including five software-engineering tasks; 17 tasks are adapted from SkillsBench and three are newly designed. Sec. 3.3 (PDF pp. 5-6) supplies each method with a task instruction and seed instance. Appendix K (PDF pp. 25-27) details manual task/skill modification and instance augmentation.
q2_assessment: A task-specific need is directly screened through no-skill failures and successful human-authored-skill runs, and measured again with the fixed solver baseline. This establishes a skill-conditioned performance gap in the curated environments, without implying that the solver lacks all underlying domain knowledge.
q2_evidence: Sec. 3.1 (PDF pp. 3-4) requires no-skill pass rates no greater than 0.5 across ten runs per instance and at least one successful run with human-authored skills. Sec. 4.1 and Table 2 (PDF pp. 6-7) use Claude Sonnet 4.6 as the fixed evaluation solver and report 10.17% no-skill versus 74.50% human-authored accuracy; Table 3 (PDF p. 8) reports the corresponding software-engineering gap of 8.00% versus 81.33%.
q3_assessment: Deterministic task outcomes support gains from generated skills over the no-skill baseline, with substantial remaining gaps to human-authored skills. Held-out variants test reuse within the same task; refinement-round results are separately limited to Productivity Tools. Skill-quality and trajectory scores are diagnostic, and the protocol does not establish preservation of unrelated capabilities or transfer across successive task types.
q3_evidence: Sec. 3.2 (PDF pp. 4-5) separates LLM-judged skill/trajectory quality from verifier-based accuracy. Appendix N.2 (PDF p. 35) requires all task tests to pass, using output assertions and functional execution checks as applicable. Tables 2-3 (PDF pp. 7-8) report overall and category outcomes; Sec. 5.2 and Fig. 2 (PDF p. 8) compare seed and held-out instances. Sec. 5.4 and Fig. 4 (PDF p. 9) test four refinement rounds only on Productivity Tools with Claude Sonnet 4.6, showing gains from teacher feedback and drift with self-feedback.

title: SWE-Bench-CL : Continual Learning for Coding Agents
core_idea: Chronological SWE-bench Verified issue streams with preliminary memory-enabled patch-generation tests; fuller continual-agent experiments and forgetting/transfer metrics are proposed
baselines: Independent-task patch generation; memory-enabled prompting; proposed LangGraph agent
metrics: Preliminary pass rate; Character Levenshtein distance; Semantic drift
metrics_display: Preliminary pass rate; Character Levenshtein distance; Semantic drift
q1_assessment: The requirements originate in real GitHub issues and fixes from SWE-bench Verified. The benchmark constructs per-repository curricula using creation time and estimated fix difficulty to study accumulated issue-resolution experience.
q1_evidence: Sec. 3.2 and Table 1 (PDF p. 3) select eight repositories and 273 tasks, order tasks primarily by creation timestamp and additionally by human fix-time categories, and record base commits, patches, test lists and overlapping modified files. Sec. 9 (PDF p. 9) limits the resulting streams to eight Python repositories and simplified sequence/dependency assumptions.
q2_assessment: Real unresolved issues define a software repair need, but the reported preliminary model results do not reliably establish a model-specific pre-update capability gap. Low independent-task pass rates are confounded by the evaluation-harness problems explicitly reported by the authors.
q2_evidence: Sec. 3.2 (PDF p. 3) includes issue statements, ground-truth fixes and FAIL_TO_PASS/PASS_TO_PASS tests. Sec. 5 and Figs. 3-4 (PDF pp. 5-6) compare independent and memory-enabled patch generation with CodeLlama-13B, Gemma-3-12B, Mistral-7B and Gemini-2.0-Flash, reporting low, variable pass rates and frequent harness failures; the authors explicitly call these results inconclusive and unreliable.
q3_assessment: The paper supports a benchmark construction and preliminary analysis of patch similarity and contextual sensitivity. Its attempted execution evaluation does not establish a reliable memory-enabled improvement, and patch distance or semantic drift cannot substitute for functional correctness. Retention and forward/backward transfer are proposed evaluation dimensions; their benefits are not established by completed continual-agent experiments in this version.
q3_evidence: Sec. 4 and Figs. 1-2 (PDF pp. 4-5) measure inter-task patch similarity and output drift under unrelated context. Sec. 5 (PDF p. 6) reports memory-enabled pass rates on par with or slightly worse than the baseline and warns that harness incompatibilities prevent reliable conclusions. Secs. 6-7 (PDF pp. 6-9) propose the interactive memory agent and retention/transfer metrics; Sec. 8 (PDF p. 9) explicitly states that full empirical evaluation is ongoing and presents its expected effects as hypotheses.

title: CodeLL : A Lifelong Learning Dataset to Support the Co-Evolution of Data and Language Models of Code
core_idea: Provides release-level longitudinal repository data so code LMs can be studied across the full software lifecycle
q1_assessment: The resource derives update requirements from the actual release histories of Python repositories. Its heuristic mappings organize real code changes for future lifelong-learning studies rather than prescribing a tested model-update curriculum.
q1_evidence: Secs. 2.1-2.3 (PDF pp. 2-3) collect 71 machine-learning-related Python repositories from Software Heritage, retain release timestamps, and map files, methods and API calls across releases. Sec. 3 (PDF p. 3) reports 2,483 releases and 970,277 Python files.
q2_assessment: The paper identifies candidate adaptation needs through repository changes, but does not measure a pre-update limitation in a particular code model. It explicitly recognizes that changed releases need not challenge a model when their distribution remains familiar.
q2_evidence: Sec. 3 and Figs. 5-6 (PDF p. 3) analyze file and method changes over Gensim releases. Sec. 4, Data distribution shift (PDF p. 4), states that code changes may not challenge language models if they do not substantially depart from the training distribution; model evaluation is presented as a research opportunity.
q3_assessment: The descriptive analyses support the dataset contribution: longitudinal traces can expose repository and API evolution. The paper does not report learned behavior change, functional validation of model outputs, capability retention or model generalization; these remain downstream uses of the resource.
q3_evidence: Sec. 3 and Figs. 3-6 (PDF p. 3) characterize release coverage and code evolution rather than model performance. Secs. 4 and 7 (PDF p. 4) propose lifelong fine-tuning, release-specific prompting and downstream applications as research opportunities or future work. Sec. 5 (PDF p. 4) limits coverage to machine-learning repositories and acknowledges heuristic mapping limitations.

title: Enhancing Continual Learning for Software Vulnerability Prediction: Addressing Catastrophic Forgetting via Hybrid-Confidence-Aware Selective Replay for Temporal LLM Fine-Tuning
core_idea: Confidence-aware selective replay picks historical exemplars by predictive uncertainty and enforces class balance in the buffer
metrics: Macro-F1; Forward F1; IBR@k; Stability Index; Training time; F1/min
metrics_display: Macro-F1; Forward F1; IBR@k; Stability Index; Training time; F1/min
q1_assessment: The stream is grounded in real CVE disclosures and their fixing commits. The experiment constructs function-level vulnerable/fixed pairs and disclosure-time windows to study temporal vulnerability prediction under changing distributions.
q1_evidence: Secs. 2.2.1-2.2.3 (PDF pp. 3-4) link 2018-2024 CVEs through CVEfixes, extract pre-fix and patched functions, deduplicate across the timeline and form 42 bi-monthly windows. Sec. 2.3.1 (PDF pp. 4-5) trains on available windows and evaluates the following window; Table 3 (PDF p. 7) lists 41 bi-monthly forward evaluation steps.
q2_assessment: The zero-shot phi-2 baseline establishes a vulnerability-classification gap, and window-only results show further room for adaptation in the evaluated stream. This does not establish that the vulnerabilities were unknown during backbone pretraining.
q2_evidence: Sec. 2.3.1 (PDF pp. 4-5) defines zero-shot, window-only and cumulative baselines. Sec. 3.2 and Table 4 (PDF pp. 7-8) report mean Macro-F1 of 0.504 for zero-shot phi-2 and 0.651 for window-only training on the 37 common comparison windows. Sec. 4.4 (PDF pp. 10-11) acknowledges possible exposure to 2018-2023 vulnerable code during phi-2 pretraining.
q3_assessment: Forward-window classification results support a small improvement from Hybrid-CASR, with separate backward-window evidence of retained vulnerability detection. Forward evaluation uses subsequent windows in the same stream; the experiments do not establish preserved general coding capability or acquisition of previously unknown vulnerability knowledge.
q3_evidence: Secs. 2.3.2 and 2.4.1 (PDF pp. 5-6) distinguish forward Macro-F1, historical-window IBR@k and across-window stability. Sec. 3.2 and Table 4 (PDF pp. 7-8) report 0.667 versus 0.651 forward F1, p = 0.026 and a small effect size. Sec. 3.3 and Table 5 (PDF p. 8) report Hybrid-CASR IBR@1/6 of 0.741/0.710 versus 0.713/0.693 for window-only. These assess classification, not generated-program execution; Sec. 4.4 (PDF pp. 10-11) limits conclusions to one architecture and the studied data.

title: CodeFlowLM: Incremental Just-In-Time Defect Prediction with Pretrained Language Models and Exploratory Insights into Defect Localization
target: Defect prediction behaviour under concept drift, class imbalance, and verification latency
core_idea: Continual LoRA fine-tuning on time-ordered commit batches with resampling and delayed-label handling; separately evaluates defect localization
base_models: CodeT5+; UniXCoder; GPT-5; Claude Sonnet 4.5; Gemini 2.5 Pro
metrics: G-Mean; Absolute class-recall gap; Recall@20%; Effort@20%; Top-k localization; Initial false alarms
metrics_display: G-Mean; Absolute class-recall gap; Recall@20%; Effort@20%; Top-k localization; Initial false alarms
q1_assessment: The update stream comes from real Java commit histories in JIT-Defects4J, with experimentally reconstructed label-availability times. Chronological batches, resampling and delayed relabeling model concept drift, evolving class imbalance and verification latency.
q1_evidence: Sec. 3.1 (PDF p. 10) orders commits chronologically and uses the first fixing commit from CommitGuru as a proxy because explicit detection timestamps are unavailable; initially clean commits can later become defect-inducing. Sec. 3.4 (PDF pp. 15-16) uses 50-commit update intervals, a 90-day waiting period for clean commits, oversampling and incremental LoRA fine-tuning.
q2_assessment: Changing labels and class distributions motivate adaptation, and the comparison establishes predictive limitations of competing incremental learners. It does not isolate the pre-update deficit of a frozen CodeT5+ or UniXCoder at each step.
q2_evidence: Sec. 3.3 (PDF pp. 12-13) selects BORB as the incremental baseline, and Sec. 3.4 (PDF pp. 15-16) compares incremental fine-tuning with its repeated retraining. Secs. 4.1.1-4.1.2 and Tables 3-4 (PDF pp. 18-19) report prequential results for these learners, without a matched no-update backbone comparison; the discussion identifies severe early class imbalance in commons-collections.
q3_assessment: Prequential classification supports effective latency-aware adaptation across the evaluated project streams, with CodeFlowLM outperforming BORB on most projects. The cross-project protocol combines earlier source-project commits with accumulating target-project data, so it supports that transfer setting. Neither the classification results nor the separate defect-localization study establish historical-task retention or retained general coding capability.
q3_evidence: Sec. 3.4 (PDF pp. 15-16) defines within-project training and cross-project updates using target history plus temporally available source commits. Sec. 4.1 and Tables 3-4 (PDF pp. 18-20) report G-Mean and class-recall gaps under prequential evaluation, with higher G-Mean in 16/19 within-project and 18/19 cross-project cases. Secs. 3.2, 3.4 and 4.2, Table 5 (PDF pp. 11-12, 16-17, 20-22), separately evaluate line rankings against labels; these are classification/localization checks, not program execution or backward retention tests.

title: Offline and Continual Just-in-Time Software Defect Prediction with Pre-trained Language Models
target: Chronological commit stream with cross-project drift and class imbalance
core_idea: Compares offline adaptation and API prompting for JIT-SDP, then evaluates continual CodeFlowLM updates using CodeT5+ and UniXCoder; other tuned models belong to offline comparisons
base_models: CodeT5+; UniXCoder; CodeReviewer; ModernBERT; LLaMA 3 8B; CodeLlama; GPT-4/4o/o1/o4-mini; Gemini 2.5 Flash
baselines: BORB; JIT-Smart; XGBoost; zero-shot/few-shot closed LLMs
metrics: F1; Precision; Recall; AUC-ROC; G-Mean; Absolute class-recall gap
edited_models: CodeT5+; UniXCoder; CodeReviewer; ModernBERT-L; ModernBERT-B; LLaMA 3 8B; CodeLlama
metrics_display: F1; Precision; Recall; AUC-ROC; G-Mean; Absolute class-recall gap
q1_assessment: The study uses real JIT-Defects4J commits for offline adaptation and constructs a chronological continual stream from the same resource. The continual requirement includes changing defect labels and class balance, with fixing-commit times used to approximate when defects become known.
q1_evidence: Sec. III-A and Table I (PDF p. 2) describe 21 open-source Java projects with commit messages, code changes and expert features. Sec. III-D, RQ4 (PDF pp. 3-4), orders commits by timestamp, estimates detection times from the first fixing commit, relabels initially clean commits and applies a 90-day waiting period before using clean commits for training.
q2_assessment: Offline zero-shot results demonstrate a task-specific prediction gap in the evaluated prompted models, including Llama 3 and CodeLlama before fine-tuning. For continual CodeT5+ and UniXCoder, the evidence compares incremental learners rather than measuring a matched frozen-backbone deficit before each update.
q2_evidence: Tables IV and VI with Sec. IV, RQs 1-2 (PDF pp. 4-5), report zero-shot F1 of 0.119/0.125 for Llama 3/CodeLlama and fine-tuned F1 of 0.425/0.407. Sec. III-D, RQ4 (PDF pp. 3-4), and Sec. IV, RQ4 with Table IX (PDF pp. 5-6), evaluate continual CodeT5+/UniXCoder against BORB using prequential classification metrics.
q3_assessment: The results support task-specific fine-tuning over the tested prompting configurations and competitive continual defect prediction. Separate offline leave-one-project-out experiments support cross-project transfer for CodeT5+ and UniXCoder. These classification evaluations do not measure backward retention on earlier tasks or preserved general coding capability.
q3_evidence: Sec. III-D (PDF p. 3) distinguishes offline fine-tuning, leave-one-project-out evaluation and the continual protocol. Tables IV-VI and VIII (PDF pp. 4-5) report prompting, fine-tuning and held-out-project results. Sec. IV, RQ4, and Table IX (PDF pp. 5-6) report prequential G-Mean and class-recall gaps, with CodeFlowLM leading BORB in 16/19 projects. These assess defect labels rather than executable code outputs; Sec. V (PDF p. 5) limits the prompting comparison by noting the absence of more sophisticated few-shot methods.

title: Retrofit: Continual Learning with Controlled Forgetting for Binary Security Detection and Analysis
target: Evolving malware threats and decompilation representation drift
core_idea: Replay-free parameter merging of legacy and newly fine-tuned teachers with low-rank/sparse update constraints and confidence-guided arbitration
baselines: CFT; LwF; PODNet; Co2L; ResAdapt; Oracle; hard/soft voting; Weight Averaging; Task Arithmetic; TIES-Merging; AdaMerging
metrics: F1; AUT; Past-Task Retention (PTR); BLEU; Exact Match; METEOR; ROUGE-L; Cross-representation average (XRep)
metrics_display: F1; Past-task retention; Temporal and representation averages; BLEU; Exact match
q1_assessment: The temporal requirement comes from real, year-ordered Android malware data. The binary-summarization experiment constructs an increasingly difficult sequence of decompilation representations to study representation drift, with historical training samples unavailable for replay.
q1_evidence: Secs. 4-5.1 (PDF pp. 7-8) use Transcendent Android applications from 2014-2018 with Drebin features and an MLP, and CAPYBARA function-documentation pairs with a CodeT5 backbone. The representation sequence uses full, anonymized and stripped decompilations; Sec. 5.1 (PDF p. 8) defines the replay-free, task-agnostic comparison.
q2_assessment: Static-model and transfer-learning comparisons directly establish an adaptation gap under the tested temporal and representation shifts. Continual fine-tuning also exposes forgetting, supporting the need for retention control without treating stage boundaries as proof of previously unknown concepts.
q2_evidence: Fig. 1 (PDF p. 2) contrasts static and continual malware detection and single-representation transfer with sequential binary summarization. Sec. 5.1 and Table 1 (PDF p. 8) define the static malware model as trained only on the first year and show its new-year F1 falling from 0.834 in 2015 to 0.425 in 2018. Sec. 5.2 (PDF pp. 8-9) reports CFT past-task retention of 0.666 after sequential updates.
q3_assessment: The experiments support improved adaptation and historical retention for malware detection, and stronger summarization across the three evaluated representations. Summarization evidence combines reference-based metrics with manual examples, rather than executable-program correctness. Generalization and preservation claims remain within these years, representations and tasks; unseen representation families and general coding retention are not established.
q3_evidence: Sec. 5.2, Fig. 4 and Table 1 (PDF pp. 8-9) evaluate old and new malware test sets and report RETROFIT PTR of 0.923 versus CFT 0.666. Sec. 5.3, Fig. 5 and Table 2 (PDF pp. 9-10) report stripped-binary BLEU of 15.05 and XRep of 25.81 across all three representations. Sec. 5.5.3 (PDF p. 12) manually examines summaries and information loss; Appendix C, Tables 3-5 (PDF p. 20), adds EM, METEOR and ROUGE-L. Sec. 6 (PDF pp. 12-13) leaves other representation shifts and downstream tasks to future work.

title: SWE-Chain: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Chained Release-Level Package Upgrades
target: Chained release-level package upgrades with inherited agent codebases
core_idea: Evaluates chained agent-modified package releases: 1660 upgrade requirements across 155 transitions in 12 chains from 9 Python packages
metrics: Resolving rate; Precision; F1; Final passing rate; Token cost
agent_backbones: Claude-Opus-4.7; Claude-Opus-4.6; Claude-Sonnet-4.6; GPT-5.5; GPT-5.4; GPT-5.3-Codex; GLM-5.1; MiniMax-M2.7-HS
metrics_display: Resolving rate; Precision; F1; Final passing rate; Token cost
q1_assessment: Upgrade requirements originate in actual package releases, release notes and implementation changes. The benchmark synthesizes structured specifications from these sources and chains the resulting upgrades through the agent-maintained codebase.
q1_evidence: Secs. 2.1-2.2 and Table 1 (PDF pp. 2-4) collect release metadata and code/test diffs, then use DecompSynth to produce 1,660 grounded requirements across 155 transitions in 12 chains from nine Python packages. Sec. 2.3 (PDF p. 4) passes each agent-produced codebase to the next upgrade; Sec. 3.2 (PDF p. 5) starts a new agent session at each step.
q2_assessment: Cross-version execution establishes a concrete software-level need for each tested upgrade behavior: the old released code fails or errors where the new version passes. Agent results additionally show incomplete upgrade capability, but do not establish that release knowledge was absent from the backbone before evaluation.
q2_evidence: Sec. 2.1, Eq. 1 (PDF p. 3), defines upgrade tests by FAIL_TO_PASS or ERROR_TO_PASS transitions between old and new gold codebases. Sec. 3.3 (PDF p. 5) also executes tests on the agent codebase before and after each step. Sec. 4.1 and Table 3 (PDF pp. 6-7) report 39.7% average Build resolving and 44.8% with one execution-error fix across nine agent-model configurations.
q3_assessment: Hidden execution tests directly assess implemented upgrade behavior and regressions in previously working non-upgrade functionality, supporting partial success and persistent maintenance failures. This is evidence about evolving software state, with preservation assessed within the package test suites. Results across 12 Python chains do not establish parameter learning, retained general model capability or transfer to untested ecosystems.
q3_evidence: Sec. 3.3 and Table 2 (PDF pp. 5-6) define resolving from upgrade-test success and precision from resolved upgrades relative to regressions in previously passing non-upgrade tests, with F1 combining them. Table 3 and Sec. 4.1 (PDF pp. 6-7) report average Build+Fix resolving/precision/F1 of 44.8%/65.4%/50.2% and final passing of 86.6%. Fig. 2 and Sec. 4.2 (PDF p. 7) show chain-specific performance. Appendix K (PDF p. 37) limits ecosystem coverage and notes no repeated sampling runs or human quality assessment of synthesized specifications.

title: CERT: Continual Pre-training on Sketches for Library-oriented Code Generation
core_idea: Continually pretrains a sketcher and generator on unlabelled library code sketches
q1_assessment: The requirement is to specialize a code model for third-party-library usage using unlabeled repository code when paired supervision is scarce. Pandas and NumPy are experimentally selected targets, with evaluation problems manually constructed from real StackOverflow questions; the study does not track API release changes.
q1_evidence: Secs. 1-3.2 (PDF pp. 2-3) motivate library-oriented generation and extract library-specific files from the whole Python pre-training corpus for sketcher/generator training. Sec. 4 (PDF pp. 3-4) constructs 101 problems each for PandasEval and NumpyEval from highly voted posts with accepted answers, followed by rewriting and programmer checks.
q2_assessment: Base-model results establish room to improve library-oriented generation for PyCodeGPT and CodeGen-mono-350M on the two benchmarks. They support specialization on these tasks, but do not establish that the libraries or API patterns were unknown before updating.
q2_evidence: Sec. 3.2 (PDF p. 3) explicitly extracts the library subcorpus from the overall pre-training corpus. Sec. 5.1 and Table 2 (PDF pp. 4-5) compare original and adapted models: PyCodeGPT pass@1 is 12.75%/18.04% on PandasEval/NumpyEval, and CodeGen is 14.24%/19.31%. The rewriting described in Sec. 4 (PDF p. 4) addresses benchmark-example exposure, not prior library knowledge.
q3_assessment: Execution-based pass@k supports improved functional performance on the crafted Pandas and NumPy problems, including problems with different numbers of API calls. Broader transfer and retention of unaffected capabilities by the library-specific models are not separately established; the HumanEval experiment evaluates the distinct general-corpus CERTg variant.
q3_evidence: Sec. 4 and the evaluation-metrics paragraph of Sec. 5 (PDF p. 4) provide 20 tests for function problems and one output check for non-function problems, counting a generation as correct only if all tests pass. Table 2 and Fig. 6 (PDF p. 5) report library-task gains and breakdowns by API count. Sec. 5.2 and Table 3 (PDF pp. 5-6) train CERTg on the whole Python corpus and compare it with PyCodeGPT on HumanEval; this is not a before/after preservation test of the library-specific CERT models.

title: CLVUL: A Contrastive Learning Framework for Unified Vulnerability Detection Localization and CWE Classification
core_idea: Aligns code and label descriptions using UniXcoder; EWC and selective freezing support new CWE stages, with replay described in the method but ambiguous in the experiment protocol
metrics: Accuracy; Precision; Recall; F1; Top-10 localization accuracy; Training time per epoch; Peak GPU memory; Throughput
metrics_display: Accuracy; F1; Top-10 localization accuracy; Time per epoch; Peak GPU memory; Throughput
q1_assessment: The motivating requirement is expansion of vulnerability categories, grounded in real C/C++ vulnerability datasets and CWE descriptions. The evaluated update stream is a constructed three-stage curriculum of 12 existing CWE categories; zero-shot recognition separately withholds selected categories from supervised training.
q1_evidence: Secs. 2.4-2.5 (PDF p. 3) define class expansion and zero-shot recognition, and Sec. 5.2 (PDF p. 6) identifies MegaVul, BigVul and Devign. Sec. 6.3 (PDF p. 9) specifies the actual three groups of four CWEs and excludes unseen-category samples from each stage; these experimental groups differ from the schematic Fig. 3 (PDF p. 5). Sec. 6.4 (PDF p. 10) fixes zero-shot targets as CWE-125 and CWE-20 in sampled MegaVul data.
q2_assessment: The evidence establishes limitations under the constructed protocol: naive sequential fine-tuning loses earlier-class performance, and simple description matching performs poorly for held-out categories. Excluding incoming CWE samples from earlier training stages does not establish that the UniXcoder backbone lacked the relevant knowledge before updating.
q2_evidence: Sec. 5.4 (PDF p. 7) identifies UniXcoder as both encoders. Sec. 6.3 and Tables 4-5 (PDF pp. 9-10) contrast current-stage-only fine-tuning with cumulative retraining and CLVUL, documenting severe earlier-class degradation for the lower bound. Sec. 6.4 and Table 6 (PDF p. 10) evaluate a known-class-trained model using direct description matching on withheld CWEs; the stage exclusion rule in Sec. 6.3 governs continual-training data, not backbone pre-training exposure.
q3_assessment: Class-wise precision, recall and F1 support adaptation to additional CWEs and better retention of earlier CWEs than naive fine-tuning, with uneven performance across categories. Separate zero-shot tests support limited recognition of the two withheld CWEs; detection and localization results assess prediction quality, not preservation of those tasks after class updates. Program execution is not required for these prediction tasks, and broader code-capability retention or deployment-wide generalization is not established.
q3_evidence: Sec. 6.3 and Tables 4-5 (PDF pp. 9-10) evaluate both earlier and newly added categories after stages 2 and 3, showing improved historical-class F1 but remaining weak categories. Sec. 6.4 and Table 6 (PDF p. 10) compare one or two withheld labels with four, six or eight trained categories and report interference as categories increase. Sec. 5.3 (PDF p. 7), Tables 2-3 (PDF pp. 7-8), and Sec. 6.2 with Fig. 9 (PDF p. 9) assess classification and ranked vulnerable-line hits separately. Sec. 8 (PDF p. 12) limits cross-project deployment claims because of distribution bias, label quality and truncation.

title: Exploring Continual Learning in Code Intelligence with Domain-wise Distilled Prompts
core_idea: Jointly updates prompts and backbone with a prompt-similarity regularizer; the separate PE-PTDD variant freezes the backbone
metrics: BLEU-4; METEOR; ROUGE-L; Precision; Recall; F1; Omega; Training time; Memory consumption
metrics_display: BLEU / METEOR / ROUGE-L; F1; Average incremental performance; Time; Memory
q1_assessment: The requirement is sequential adaptation to different code domains while retaining earlier-domain performance without replay. The streams are experimentally constructed from existing project partitions for summarization and vulnerability detection, and algorithm groups for clone detection; they do not represent dated software changes.
q1_evidence: Sec. 2.1 (PDF pp. 2-3) defines domain-incremental learning with unknown domain identity at test time and access only to current training data. Sec. 4.1 (PDF p. 4) splits each CodeSearchNet language and Big-Vul into five project groups, and partitions the 104 POJ algorithms into five groups with sampled clone pairs.
q2_assessment: Sequential fine-tuning and vanilla prompt-tuning baselines demonstrate forgetting for CodeT5 summarization and CodeBERT vulnerability/clone detection under the selected domain streams. The experiments do not separately establish an incoming domain as a capability absent from the pre-trained model before each update.
q2_evidence: Secs. 4.2 and 5.1 (PDF pp. 4-6) specify the task backbones and sequential fine-tuning/prompt-tuning comparisons. Fig. 3 and the discussion in Secs. 5.1-5.2 (PDF pp. 6-7) show declining first-dataset and previously learned-dataset scores as new datasets arrive; Sec. 2.1 (PDF p. 3) defines evaluation after learning on seen datasets, rather than a pre-update incoming-domain competence test.
q3_assessment: The results support better sequential task performance and reduced forgetting on the tested domains, with explicit historical-dataset evaluation. Omega combines current and earlier task scores and does not isolate forgetting; summarization overlap and classification metrics assess these non-executable outputs. The study does not separately establish transfer to untrained domains or retention of unrelated code capabilities, and low-resource experiments remain within the same task streams.
q3_evidence: Sec. 3.2 and Algorithm 1 (PDF p. 4) jointly update prompts and backbone, with backbone freezing reserved for PE-PTDD. Sec. 4.3 and Eq. (8) (PDF p. 5) define BLEU/METEOR/ROUGE-L, classification precision/recall/F1, and Omega over all seen test sets and stages. Tables 1-2 and Sec. 5.2 (PDF pp. 5-6) report gains, while Fig. 3 (PDF p. 7) separately tracks the first dataset and averages over seen datasets. Sec. 5.5 and Table 3 (PDF pp. 7-8) reduce training samples but keep the validation/test sets unchanged; Sec. 7 (PDF p. 10) limits evidence to the two backbones and five-part datasets.

title: Learning Never Stops: Improving Software Vulnerability Type Identification via Incremental Learning
core_idea: Incremental learning for continually emerging vulnerability type labels
metrics: Accuracy; Precision; Recall; Macro-F1; MCC; Training time
benchmark: Self-built NVD/CVE vulnerability-type dataset: 6269 vulnerabilities, 992 projects, 23 CWE types
metrics_display: Accuracy; Precision; Recall; Macro-F1; MCC; Training time
q1_assessment: The requirement comes from continuously reported vulnerabilities and their imbalanced CWE types in real NVD/CVE-linked software histories. The experiment simulates incremental type identification by partitioning a curated C/C++ dataset into five commit-time-ordered tasks; temporal order defines the stream without proving that later knowledge was absent from pre-training.
q1_evidence: Sec. 4.2 and Fig. 3 (PDF p. 7) describe collecting NVD CVEs, linking fixing commits, extracting functions and filtering labels to obtain 6,269 vulnerabilities from 992 projects across 23 CWE types. Secs. 3.1 and 4.5 (PDF pp. 4, 8) define five tasks ordered by vulnerability commit time and 80/10/10 training/validation/test partitions.
q2_assessment: Sequential baseline comparisons establish a task-performance gap, including poor identification of rare CWE types, in the constructed temporal stream. They do not provide a separate pre-update measurement on each incoming task or establish that those vulnerability types were previously unknown to the target backbone.
q2_evidence: Secs. 4.3-4.5 (PDF p. 8) train the comparison methods under the five-task protocol and evaluate the final model across task test sets. Sec. 5.1 and Tables 1-2 (PDF p. 9) report overall and rare-CWE performance below VulTypeIL; Sec. 6.1 and Table 8 (PDF p. 11) compare prompt tuning with a CodeT5 fine-tuning variant. These are trained-method comparisons, not a frozen-model before/after test for every temporal transition.
q3_assessment: Classification results support improved vulnerability-type identification, including rare classes, and historical-task evaluation supplies retention evidence within the stream. The final averages mix recent and earlier tasks, so they do not isolate the amount of forgetting; execution is not required for this classification task. Repeating experiments on Big-Vul broadens dataset coverage but does not demonstrate transfer of an already updated model, and unrelated code capabilities are not tested.
q3_evidence: Sec. 3.1 (PDF p. 4) evaluates test sets S1 through Si after task i; Sec. 4.4 (PDF p. 8) defines final-model averages across all tasks for accuracy, precision, recall, macro-F1 and MCC. Tables 1-2 (PDF p. 9) report overall and rare-type gains, and Secs. 5.2-5.3 with Tables 3-5 (PDF pp. 9-10) compare regularization, replay and loss variants. Sec. 5.5 and Table 7 (PDF p. 11) compare backbone choices. Sec. 6.5 and Table 14 (PDF pp. 12-13) repeat the method comparison on Big-Vul; Sec. 6.6 (PDF p. 13) limits representativeness primarily to C/C++ vulnerabilities.

title: Towards Prompt Tuning-based Software Vulnerability Assessment with Continual Learning
core_idea: Hybrid prompt tuning with confidence-based replay and EWC for successive severity-prediction tasks
q1_assessment: The requirement is continued vulnerability-severity assessment using real C/C++ vulnerability records, descriptions and CVSS 3.0 labels. The five sequential tasks are experimentally partitioned from a MegaVul-derived dataset; their construction does not establish a chronological deployment stream.
q1_evidence: Secs. 3.1 and 4.2 (PDF pp. 3, 6) describe selecting vulnerable functions from MegaVul, collecting CVSS 3.0-aligned severity information and using code plus vulnerability descriptions to predict four severity levels. The original dataset is split into five tasks, with random 80/10/10 training/validation/test splits within each task; no time-ordering rule is specified for the task sequence.
q2_assessment: The sequential CWMXGB baseline demonstrates loss on the first severity task, and trained-method comparisons show room to improve severity prediction. These findings motivate adaptation and retention in the selected partitions, but do not separately measure CodeT5 or CodeBERT competence on each incoming partition before updating.
q2_evidence: Sec. 4.4 (PDF p. 7) adapts the five SVA baselines to the sequential protocol. Sec. 5.1 and Figs. 3-4 (PDF p. 8) report baseline performance and declining first-task F1/MCC for CWMXGB as later tasks are learned. Secs. 5.4-5.5 and Figs. 8-9 (PDF pp. 9-10) compare trained CodeT5/CodeBERT and prompt-tuning/fine-tuning variants, rather than unadapted incoming-task measurements.
q3_assessment: Macro-F1 and macro-MCC support improved severity prediction across the five tasks, and first-task trajectories provide direct evidence of retained or improved historical-task performance. Execution is not required for severity classification. Preservation of unrelated code abilities and generalization beyond this dataset and partition protocol are not separately evaluated.
q3_evidence: Sec. 3.1 (PDF p. 3) reevaluates all seen task test sets after each update, while Sec. 4.3 and Eqs. (17)-(18) (PDF p. 7) average final-model scores across task test sets. Sec. 5.1 and Figs. 3-4 (PDF p. 8) report aggregate gains and first-task retention. Sec. 5.3 and Figs. 6-7 (PDF p. 9) compare EWC and confidence-based replay variants; Sec. 5.4 and Fig. 8 (PDF pp. 9-10) compare CodeT5 and CodeBERT. Sec. 6.2 (PDF pp. 10-11) identifies dataset construction and adapted baselines as validity boundaries.

title: Code2LoRA: Hypernetwork-Generated Adapters for Code Language Models under Software Evolution
target: Repository import/API/convention knowledge under software evolution
core_idea: Hypernetwork generates repository-specific LoRA adapters with zero inference tokens; Code2LoRA-Evo updates adapters via a GRU hidden state on each code diff
baselines: Pretrained; RAG (k=3); Dep.-Resolved Context; FFT; Single LoRA; Per-repo LoRA; Text2LoRA
metrics: Exact Match; Edit Similarity; CodeBLEU; Adaptation time; Token cost
benchmark: RepoPeftBench: static and evolution assertion-completion tracks
metrics_display: Exact Match; Edit Similarity; CodeBLEU; Adaptation time; Token cost
q1_assessment: The update requirement comes from real repository evolution, represented by production-code diffs and assertions added or modified in Git histories. RepoPeftBench constructs assertion-completion probes from these test suites and separately evaluates snapshot adaptation, chronological evolution and held-out repositories.
q1_evidence: Sec. 4 (PDF p. 5) builds the benchmark from 604 Python repositories, forms prefix/expected-value assertion pairs, and emits evolution-track tasks when commits add or modify assertions, paired with production-code diffs. In-repository evolution splits order training before validation/test; cross-repository splits hold repositories out entirely. Appendix B.3 (PDF p. 13) details prefix extraction and quality filters; Sec. 3.3 (PDF p. 4) updates the repository state recurrently from incoming diffs.
q2_assessment: Unadapted Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B results directly establish an assertion-completion gap on the tested repositories. Comparisons with static adapters on the same evolution-track inputs additionally support a need to account for changing repository state, without requiring that all underlying APIs were unfamiliar before updating.
q2_evidence: Sec. 5 (PDF p. 6) identifies the common backbone and Pretrained baseline. Tables 2-3 and Secs. 6.1-6.2 (PDF pp. 6-8) report original-model EM of 45.7%/46.8% on static cross-/in-repository tests and 31.5%/29.3% on evolution tests; on the latter, Code2LoRA-Static obtains 55.7%/60.6% versus Evo at 60.3%/64.5%. These same-track comparisons establish the adaptation gap more directly than temporal ordering alone.
q3_assessment: EM, edit similarity and CodeBLEU support better assertion-reference agreement under repository adaptation, with separate cross-repository and temporal-holdout evidence of generalization. Main results do not establish full execution correctness; the paper mentions a runnable-slice execution probe and leaves comprehensive runtime evaluation outside its scope. Performance along commit histories measures the evolving target distribution, not retention on fixed earlier tasks or unrelated code capabilities.
q3_evidence: Sec. 5 (PDF p. 6) defines reference-based metrics; Tables 2-4 (PDF pp. 7-8) compare static, evolution and OOD performance. Sec. 6.3 (PDF p. 8) evaluates 92 repositories created after the cutoff and limits interpretation to within-OOD comparisons because shorter targets inflate EM. The Limitations section (PDF p. 9) mentions a pytest-based probe on a runnable CR-test slice and states that executing every generated assertion was out of scope. Appendix F.3 and Fig. 9 (PDF pp. 19-20) bin current assertion scores by commit position, without reevaluating fixed historical tasks; the stated evaluation scope is one Python assertion task and one backbone (PDF p. 9).
